definition: An attack where the token header chooses the signing algorithm. The attacker signs with HMAC (HS256) using the issuer's public key as the secret, and a validator that lets the header pick the algorithm accepts it. The stub validator allows ES256 only and rejects none and HMAC before looking up any key.

The claim naming which resource a token is meant for. A resource server must check that its own identifier is in aud, otherwise a token issued for another API works everywhere. The wrong-token tester sends a wrong-audience token and a token meant for a downstream API (RFC 8707 passthrough) and expects 401 invalid_token for both.

Decoding a JWT only reads its Base64URL parts, and anyone can write any claims. In this app a decode reports the signature as not_verified unless you ask to verify, and then only tokens signed by the app's own stub key are valid; a token from a real issuer cannot be verified because the tool never fetches a real JWKS.

Demonstrating Proof of Possession (RFC 9449): the client signs a proof with its own key and the access token is bound to that key's thumbprint in the cnf claim, so a stolen token is useless without the key. In the flow catalog this is a simulation; in the tester, cnf is decoded and explained but not enforced by the stub resource server.

When a check cannot be completed, or any check fails, the token is refused. The stub validator names the rule that rejected the token (alg, kid, signature, iss, exp, nbf, aud, actor, scope), and a checker run against an unreachable target marks every rule as error rather than pass.

A simplified reading of the FAPI 2.0 profile written for this demo. It is not a conformance suite and has not been checked against the FAPI 2.0 text line by line. Do not use its result to say a product is or is not FAPI 2.0 compliant.

Six mechanisms (PKCE, PAR, RAR, DPoP, mTLS, JAR) run as mock flows with and without their protection. Keys and certificates are generated per run, no TLS is performed, and each attack outcome is computed by a small in-memory check (hash compare or signature verify). It illustrates why a protection works; it does not run the real protocols and models no product.

Every string that comes back from a token or a target (claim values, kid, metadata, error text) is treated as data: hidden and control characters are shown as [U+XXXX], sizes are bounded, and the UI renders it as a text node, never as HTML.

JWT-Secured Authorization Request (RFC 9101): the authorization request parameters are signed so the server can tell they were not changed on the way. Shown here as a simulated flow with and without the protection.

The only mode. The authorization-server stubs, the resource server and the issuer all run inside this process on loopback ports 5911-5916. The checker and tester accept loopback http targets only; there is no live mode, no tenant and no network.

Probes an authorization server (one of five bundled stubs, or a loopback server you run) with rule-by-rule requests such as unregistered redirect URI, authorization code without PKCE, password grant and double code redemption, and reports pass or fail with evidence per rule.

Pushed Authorization Requests (RFC 9126): the client sends the authorization request directly to the server and the browser carries only a short request_uri, so the parameters cannot be edited in the URL. Shown as a simulated flow with and without the protection.

Proof Key for Code Exchange (RFC 7636): the party that starts the flow keeps a one-time code_verifier and sends its S256 hash. A stolen authorization code cannot be redeemed without the verifier. It does not authenticate the client and does not bind the access token.

Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396): authorization_details describe exactly what is allowed (type, amount, recipient) instead of a broad scope. The resource server still has to compare each request with them.

The checker's rules for the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice. The rule texts are this demo's paraphrase, and only RFC numbers are cited, not section numbers, because the sections were not checked against the RFC text.

An access token bound to a key or certificate (cnf with a DPoP key thumbprint or an mTLS certificate thumbprint) so only the holder of that key can use it. The decode view explains the binding; the stub resource server does not enforce it.

Sends fifteen tokens, one correct control and fourteen wrong ones, to a stub MCP-style resource server and shows the expected and actual status, the WWW-Authenticate error, the check that rejected it and a lesson for each. If the control fails, every other result is meaningless.

The header a resource server sends with a 401 or 403. With no token it carries no error code and points to the protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728); with a bad token it carries error="invalid_token"; with a valid token that lacks permission, 403 and error="insufficient_scope" (RFC 6750).
